subject: history
title: Nicholas II and the 1905 Revolution
welcome_lead: Autocracy under strain: war, Bloody Sunday and constitutional compromise.
meta_desc: A-Level Russia 1894-1924 adventure on Nicholas II, Russo-Japanese War, Bloody Sunday and the 1905 Revolution.
final_note: You can explain why 1905 was a 'dress rehearsal' rather than a revolution.

concepts.def: Last Tsar of Russia 1894-1917, committed to autocracy; abdicated on 15 March 1917 (New Style).
Conflict ending in Russian defeat at Tsushima (May 1905); Treaty of Portsmouth September 1905.
Massacre on 22 January 1905 of unarmed petitioners led by Father Gapon outside the Winter Palace.
Nicholas II's promise of civil rights and an elected Duma, drafted by Witte to defuse the general strike.
Constitution issued 23 April 1906 reserving autocratic prerogatives and undermining the Duma.
Prime Minister 1906-11 combining harsh repression ('Stolypin necktie') with agrarian reforms; assassinated September 1911.

walkthroughs.body_html: Nicholas II succeeded Alexander III in November 1894, calling reform 'senseless dreams'. Industrialisation under Witte brought urbanisation and the rise of new parties: Social Democrats (1898; split into Bolsheviks/Mensheviks 1903), Socialist Revolutionaries (1901) and Liberals/Kadets. The 'small victorious war' against Japan turned into humiliation: Port Arthur fell in January 1905 and the fleet was destroyed at Tsushima in May 1905.

On 22 January 1905, troops fired on Father Gapon's petitioners outside the Winter Palace, killing roughly 200. Strikes, naval mutinies (the Potemkin) and the Petersburg Soviet (October) followed. The October Manifesto (17 October 1905) split opposition: Liberals largely accepted it. The Moscow uprising (December 1905) was crushed.

The Fundamental Laws (April 1906) preceded the First Duma, dismissed within months. The Second was dissolved in June 1907 and Stolypin's electoral law produced a tamer Third (1907-12) and Fourth (1912-17). Stolypin's agrarian reforms (1906-11) abolished redemption payments and allowed peasants to leave the commune. About 2 million did so by 1914.
